statements.quote: The poetry system was trained exclusively on a corpus of standard, nonpoetic text—derived from the CommonCrawl corpus (https:// commo ncrawl. org/). After a series of filtering rules were applied to this vast and generic corpus of text (e.g. retain only sentences written in English that are 20 words or less), the resulting corpus from which the poetry generation system was trained on contains 500 million words in total, which is constructed from a vocabulary of 15 thousand unique words.

statements.quote: In both studies, integrating the poetry generation system with our web application (URL link) required both back- and front-end development. For our back-end framework, we chose  Flask[68] —a small and lightweight Python web framework that provides useful tools and features that make creating web applications in Python more convenient. The programming language adopted for this is Python. To record and store data submitted by participants, Firebase was utilized. Firebase is a platform developed by Google that not only facilitates data storage, but also enables the development of mobile and web applications. We opted to use Google Cloud Platform (GCP) as our server and Gunicorn for deployment. Gunicorn is a widely used high-performance Python WSGI HTTP Server based on the UNIX system. For front-end development, we mainly used Jinja2 to implement our functions (e.g., login verification, submission of forms) and facilitate asynchronous transfers (data exchange between back- and front-end). Jinja2 is a full-featured template engine for Python. The interface we developed is built on Bulma—a free, open-source framework that provides ready-to-use front-end components that can be combined to build responsive web interfaces. More complicated components and functions required jQuery and AJAX. The programming languages we adopted for front-end development were HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML is adopted to provide the basic structure of our web application, which in turn is enhanced and modified via the use of CSS and JavaScript. CSS is used to control presentation, formatting, and layout. JavaScript is used to control the execution of specialized functions (e.g., imposing time constraints on webpages).
statements.locator: p. 9, Methods, paragraph on development of the experimental web application and recording participant data; Markdown line 229.

deposits.notes:
Single project cited three times in the paper and in both form.data_and_code URL fields. Project title: 'Establishing the Importance of Self-Efficacy in Creative Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence'. Anonymous public GETs to the landing page, node metadata, OSF Storage listing, and children listing all returned HTTP 200. Node metadata explicitly reports public=true and node_license=null.

Complete inventory: three root files, no subfolders, zero children, zero linked nodes, zero wiki pages, and OSF Storage is the only storage provider (all listing endpoints HTTP 200; no next pages). All three files downloaded successfully with HTTP 200, below 20 MB, and were read only in memory. Syntax PDF has two pages covering the Study 1 t-test/ANOVA and Study 2 ANOVAs/PROCESS models. No interface source code, separate raw expert ratings, draft poems, or participant-flow file is deposited.

rows_checked=298 is the combined number of rows in the two SAV files: S1 has 146 rows (96 people and 50 AI-only benchmark poems), and S2 has 152 rows (152 people). Thus 248 participant rows, not 298 participants. There is no participant-ID column; each human row holds that participant's one poem, condition, and outcome scores, so no cross-file linkage is needed for within-study arm summaries or poem diversity.

S1: CreativeCollabAI_Study1.sav has 146 rows and 13 columns. condition_coded=1 has 48 human-alone rows, =2 has 48 human-AI editor rows, and =3 has 50 AI-only benchmark rows. These arm names are inferred from matching the printed Table 1 score means and from the missing age/self-report fields in the 50 benchmark rows; the SAV has no variable/value labels. Expert_creativity is present on all 146 rows; self_creativity is present on all 96 human rows. AC is 'study' or 'Study' for all 96 people and blank for all benchmark rows. No excluded human rows or exclusion flags are present. The data confirm the analyzed sample, but cannot reconcile the paper's 101 recruited minus 6 excluded with 96 analyzed, establish original randomized arm counts, or establish exclusion timing.

S2: CreativeCollabAI_Study2.sav has 152 rows and 15 columns. condition is a string: '1'=human alone (51), '2'=human-AI editor (50), '3'=co-creator human-AI (51). Mapping is corroborated by the printed Table 2 means and the dummy_1/dummy_2 coding described in the paper's mediation section. expert_creativity, creativity_self, creative_selfeff, and all three self-efficacy items are nonmissing on every row. dummy_1 intentionally excludes condition '1' and dummy_2 excludes condition '2'; these missing values do not indicate missing outcomes.

Text completeness matters: poem is nonempty for all 146 S1 and 152 S2 rows. S1's SPSS format is A255, and inspected strings visibly stop mid-word or mid-sentence. All 48 editor and 50 AI-only texts have stored lengths of 254 or 255 characters; 15 of the 48 human-alone texts have length 255. These are incomplete texts, so the available fragments are unsuitable for treating S1 as a complete-poem diversity dataset. S2's poem format is A807; its 101 AI-arm entries all parse in memory as lists of exactly eight strings, and the 51 human-alone entries are multiline text. No comparable truncation was apparent in the S2 checks. Normalize these differing text representations before diversity analysis.

Only one expert-creativity composite per poem is supplied. Neither SAV nor the syntax PDF explains how the individual poets' ratings were combined; inter-rater reliability and alternative rater aggregation cannot be reconstructed. Original AI drafts and editing histories are absent, so editing extent cannot be computed from the final poem alone.

Data-derived verification, not additional printed paper statistics: S2 human expert-creativity sample SD is 4.9759752026124975, supporting Table 2's 4.98 rather than the narrative's 9.24. Recomputing the S1 three-group ANOVA from all 146 deposited expert scores gives F(2,143)=62.25392103642393, which still differs from the paper's F(2,145)=63.48. The deposit therefore permits checking that discrepancy but does not resolve its origin.

License is null because no dataset license is specified in the OSF metadata or a license file. The article's license does not establish the terms for the deposited data.

what_we_could_compute: Open question 6: compute arm-specific analyzed n, means, sample SDs, and SEs from one score per participant in both studies; compute two-arm creativity contrasts and their SEs and standardized effects. For S1 participant inference, omit condition_coded=3 (50 AI-only poems) rather than using it in the participant contrast's error term.

Open question 3: verify S1 analyzed counts (48 human alone and 48 editor), distinguish its 50 AI-only benchmark rows, and recompute the three-group ANOVA. The posted rows cannot establish recruited/randomized counts or explain the published count and F-test discrepancies.
Open question 5: resolve S2's conflicting human-arm expert-creativity SD directly from the data (4.9759752026124975, which rounds to the Table 2 value 4.98).
Open question 8: count S2 poems and outcome records directly: 152 total, with arm counts 51/50/51.

Compute S2 within-arm and between-arm text/idea diversity from the final poems, preserving row-level association with condition and creativity scores. S1 permits only analyses of its stored, often truncated text fragments; it does not support an unqualified full-poem diversity comparison.

Open questions 4, 9, and 10 remain limited: no excluded participant rows or original assignment log, no initial AI drafts/edit histories, and no separate rater scores are available. Exclusion timing and original randomized counts, amount of editing, the expert-rating aggregation rule, and inter-rater reliability cannot be reconstructed from this deposit.
notes:
Checked 2026-10-09. Read all 422 lines (57,080 characters) of the saved Markdown conversion, covering all 11 PDF pages through the end matter. The saved file has no appendices or supplementary-material section and contains no preregistration statement. Availability and provenance quotations were checked against PDF text extracted with PyMuPDF. Quotations in this record are copied from the Markdown source, retaining its URL spacing and citation markup where present; Markdown emphasis around headings is removed.

Status is public_participant_data because the OSF files were downloaded anonymously and their participant rows, conditions, and creativity-score columns were inspected directly with pyreadstat.read_sav(io.BytesIO(...)). The S1 text truncation, absent excluded cases, absent separate rater scores, and absent original drafts do not negate availability of participant-level outcomes but limit the additional analyses specified below.

The paper's 'requests for materials' sentence is a correspondence instruction, not a statement that these study data require a request. No login, account creation, contact with authors, or access request was made. No file other than forms/data/c096.json was created or changed.

No additional matching deposit was identified by the recorded searches. Broad surname searches were narrowed rather than exhaustively paginated; OSF's supplied search endpoint filters titles rather than author names. The publisher landing page and DOI resolver returned HTTP 200 with a Client Challenge bot check, so publisher supplementary material could not be inspected. No effort was made to pass that challenge.

Other paper links were checked and are not deposits of these randomized studies: https://commoncrawl.org/ (HTTP 200; training-corpus source), https://www.nus.edu.sg/research/irb/resources/references (200), http://www.prolific.ac (200, redirects to https://www.prolific.com/), http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1038/s41598-024-69423-2&domain=pdf (200), https://hbr.org/2023/04/how-generative-ai-could-disrupt-creative-work (200), https://hbr.org/2023/06/boost-your-productivity-with-generative-ai (200), and http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/ (200). The exact printed reference links http://arXiv.org/2301.04655, http://arXiv.org/2309.14556, http://arXiv.org/2309.05196, http://arXiv.org/2212.09251, http://arXiv.org/2303.12767, and http://arXiv.org/2307.09009 each returned 404; they cite other papers, not this study's deposit. https://www.nature.com/reprints and https://www.nature.com/scientificreports/ each returned HTTP 200 Client Challenge pages and were not pursued.
